newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Weak exports could signal lower Singapore growth.
newsitem.headline: Weak exports could signal lower Singapore growth.

text.p: Singapore's full year growth could fall below forecasts after a sharp fall in February non-oil exports, with a electronics trough continuing into the second half of the year, economists said on Monday.
Several said they would revise full year gross domestic product (GDP) down to about 7 percent, at the top end of the government's conservative prediction of growth of between five and seven percent.
A Reuter poll of 16 financial institutions last week, before a sharp 7.9 percent drop in February domestic non-oil exports was announced, predicted GDP for the full-year at 7.3 percent.
The fourth consecutive month of export decline was blamed on a fall in disk drive exports.
"The Seagate shift in low-end disk drive manufacturing to China partly explains why Singapore saw such a drop in output," Liew Yin Sze, economist with J.M. Sassoon said.
Seagate said on Friday that exports, calculated on a three month moving average, fell between 4 and 6 percent in February due to its shift of desktop drives making to China.
The company is investing US$32 million in a new building in the Wuxi-Singapore Industrial Park in China to expand disk drive capacity.
Liew said this amounted to a permanent loss for Singapore and would delay end of the electronic slump until mid-year.
"It will probably be the worst quarter for manufacturing, but there are some sectors that will help shore it up," Liew said, adding that services and construction would do well.
Even before the sharply lower February export number, many economists were prepared to lower their forecasts for the first quarter due to excess supplies and slow demand.
"The first quarter will be weaker than expected because inventory correction is still taking place," said Violet Soh, research manager with Fraser Securities.
"There is still no recovery in sight," she said. But Soh said she was sticking by earlier projections that recovery would feature in the second half of the year.
The 16 economists polled by Reuters produced an average prediiction of 1.5 percent growth in February non-oil expports.
But with manufacturing still limping along and U.S. orders for electronic components not lending support yet, economists said first quarter GDP would be worse than the fourth quarter of 1996.
"The first quarter should be below 4.0 percent and this will bring down the average for the full year unless the second half is sharply higher," said Nikko Research economist Gan Chin Lee.
Gan said he would lower the year-on-year GDP for 1997 to 7.0 from 7.3 percent.
He said the trade data raised fresh concerns Singapore's export-dependent economy would limp along for a while.
A recovery might be supported later in the year by a weaker Singapore dollar and regional factors, such a South Korean loss of exports after labour strikes earlier this year.
"A weaker currency will help but this will not be translated into stronger exports in the immediate term. It will take three or four months," Gan said.
